opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. My short answer is that neural graphics won't replace ray tracing. It's going to change what ray tracing is *for*.

Think about what ray tracing really is. It's a way of answering a very physical question: where does light go, and what does it hit? That question doesn't go away just because we have neural networks. Light transport is still governed by physics. Visibility, occlusion and reflection still have to come from somewhere.

What neural methods are really good at is the part where we've traditionally been brute-forcing things. Take path tracing. You shoot a huge number of rays, most of them are noisy, and you average them out. That's expensive. Neural denoisers, neural radiance caches and learned importance sampling all let you get away with far fewer samples. So in a sense, ray tracing becomes the "ground truth signal" and the neural network becomes the "reconstruction engine." We already see this with real-time denoising and upscaling in games. You trace maybe one ray per pixel, sometimes less, and the network fills in the rest.

Longer term, I see a kind of hybrid stack. Some parts of a scene might be represented explicitly, like triangles and materials, and some implicitly, like neural fields or Gaussian representations. Ray tracing, or more generally ray *querying*, becomes the universal interface that lets you ask questions of both. You march a ray through a neural field, or you intersect it with geometry, and you combine the answers.

The other thing I care about, coming from the simulation and compiler side, is differentiability. Once your renderer is differentiable, ray tracing isn't just for producing images anymore. It becomes a tool for *inverse* problems: reconstructing geometry, materials and lighting from photos, or optimizing designs. That's where graphics, vision and machine learning really merge. The programming systems have to support that well. You want to write the physics clearly and have the gradients, the parallelism and the performance handled for you.

So my view is that ray tracing moves from being the whole pipeline to being the physically grounded backbone, with learned components wrapped around it. The networks handle the approximation and the data-driven priors. The rays keep everything honest.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says neural graphics “won’t replace ray tracing.”

r002.rationale: It describes neural denoising and upscaling from sparse ray samples in games, but does not identify DLSS or explain its reconstruction specifically.

r003.rationale: It proposes ray querying neural fields alongside geometry, not rendering directly from a voxel representation without ray tracing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing that neural graphics replaces ray tracing, because I think over the long term they fuse into one pipeline rather than one winning.

Ray tracing is fundamentally a very clean statement of the physics: light leaves a source, bounces around, some of it reaches a sensor. The hard part has never been the formulation, it's been the cost. Monte Carlo path tracing is embarrassingly simple and embarrassingly expensive. So for decades the field has been building clever ways to spend fewer samples, and neural methods are, in my view, the most powerful tool we've ever had for that specific problem. Neural denoising, neural radiance caching, learned importance sampling, neural materials that compress a huge measured BRDF into a tiny network. All of that keeps ray tracing as the backbone and just makes it dramatically cheaper. I'd expect that trend to continue: the renderer stays physically grounded, and the network fills in what you'd otherwise pay for with brute force.

The second direction is more radical, which is representing the scene itself neurally, things in the NeRF and Gaussian splatting family. There the role of ray tracing changes from "the rendering algorithm" to "the query interface." You still march a ray through space, you still ask what radiance arrives along this direction, but what's on the other end of the query is a learned function instead of triangles and a BRDF. And honestly I find that elegant. The ray is a universal abstraction, and it doesn't care whether the thing it hits is a mesh or a network.

What I don't think happens is that we throw away the physics and have a model hallucinate frames end to end for serious work. Artists and engineers need controllability, consistency across frames, correct shadows and reflections under novel lighting. Purely generative approaches are getting better fast, but when you need something to be right rather than plausible, having a differentiable, physically based renderer in the loop is the thing that keeps you honest. And that word, differentiable, is really the bridge. Once your ray tracer can compute gradients, it stops being a black box you run at the end and becomes a layer you can train through. That's where my own work with Taichi and differentiable simulation has pulled me, and I think it's where the two worlds genuinely meet.

So long term: ray tracing becomes less of a monolithic algorithm and more of a substrate. Neural components sit inside it for efficiency, sit beside it as scene representations, and sit on top of it as optimization loops. The ray survives. It just gets a lot of new neighbors.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly rejects ray tracing being replaced, predicting that neural graphics and ray tracing will fuse and that “the ray survives.”

r002.rationale: It mentions neural denoising and efficiency, but does not explain DLSS or describe reconstructing an image from sparsely rendered samples.

r003.rationale: It discusses neural scene representations, but does not propose rendering directly from a voxel representation or eliminating ray tracing.

astra-6.text:
I think, over the long term, neural graphics will change how much work we ask ray tracing to do. Instead of explicitly tracing every path, we can use a neural network to estimate parts of the image that would otherwise be very expensive to compute.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean ray tracing disappears. It can still provide the reference images for training, or handle cases where we need more accurate light transport. The challenge for a learned method is whether it remains reliable when you change the scene, the lighting, or the materials.

So I would expect a hybrid approach: ray tracing provides a physically grounded foundation, and neural methods help us get to a good image with much less computation. Over time, the balance could shift toward more learned computation, depending on how much accuracy and control the application needs.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a hybrid approach and says ray tracing does not necessarily disappear; it does not clearly predict eventual replacement.

r002.rationale: It does not mention DLSS or explain reconstruction from sparsely rendered samples.

r003.rationale: It mentions neural estimation of expensive image computations, but not rendering directly from a scene’s voxel representation without ray tracing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think neural graphics and ray tracing are complementary. Ray tracing gives us a physically grounded way to simulate how light moves through a scene, but doing all of that computation for every pixel is expensive. Neural networks can help reconstruct an image from fewer samples, or approximate parts of the light transport that are particularly costly.

Over the long term, I expect more hybrid systems. We’ll trace rays where accuracy matters and use learned methods where we can make a good approximation. That could shift the role of ray tracing: it becomes both a rendering tool and a way to generate training data or validate what a neural model predicts.

The interesting question is how much control and reliability we can preserve. A beautiful image is one thing; getting predictable results when you change the lighting, materials, or geometry is another. I think that’s where physics-based methods will continue to be valuable.

r001.rationale: The response predicts hybrid systems in which ray tracing remains useful, rather than saying neural graphics will eventually replace it.

r002.rationale: It mentions neural networks reconstructing images from fewer samples, but does not identify DLSS or explain its use of data-driven reconstruction.

r003.rationale: It does not propose rendering directly from a scene’s voxel representation; it describes using learned methods alongside ray tracing.
